To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

tenosynovial inflammation is a common early finding on MRI in CSA patients who develop RA, and that the number of locations affected by inflammation, and the presence of MCP extensor tendon inflammation are the most important MRI features to predict RA development in patients with CSA.
the presence of tenosynovial inflammation, particularly MCP-extensors, and the number of affected locations are predictive for RA development in CSA patients.

tenosynovial inflammation is among the first tissue affected in RA, that this inflammation is located at the extensor side of the MCP joints, and that the number of locations of subclinical inflammation can improve the prediction for RA development.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a search to the target tissues in which RA-specific subclinical inflammation starts.
the identification of the tissue in which RA specific inflammation starts, and how this can be used to identify patients at highest risk to develop RA.
the identification of the target tissue in the early stages of the development of RA, and the identification of the first locations of inflammation in the target tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
tenosynovial inflammation is the first tissue involved in RA, but not the only one.
the combination of MCP-extensor tendinitis and the number of affected locations with synovitis or bone marrow edema is predictive for RA in CSA patients.
the MCP extensor tenosynovium is one of the first sites of RA-specific inflammation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MCP-extensor tendon complex is the target tissue in the early phase of RA, and that this complex is a good target to detect RA in the clinically suspect phase.

we have shown that the presence of MCP-extensors peritendinitits is a very early feature of RA and that the number of locations in which subclinical inflammation is present, also improves the prediction for RA development.
RA-specific inflammation starts in the extensor tendons, and that the more joints and tendons involved, the greater the risk of RA development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
RA-specific inflammation starts in the target tissue, i.e. the tendon sheath, and that the number of locations affected by subclinical inflammation is an important determinant for RA prediction.
